citation.title: The Determinants and Importance of States’ Attendance at Conferences of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)
citation.venue_or_publisher: Paper submitted to the 9th Annual Conference on the Political Economy of International Organizations (PEIO), September 30, 2015
citation.type: conference paper, draft (title page: "Draft. Please do not cite without permission.")

question: What explains variation in member states' delegation sizes at the UNFCCC COPs in 1995-2014, and does delegation size affect a state's access to Global Environmental Facility (GEF) funds? Quote p2: "analyzes the variation in member states’ attendance at the UNFCCC’s Conferences of the Parties (COPs) in 1995-2014". It does not ask about business or fossil-fuel presence in delegations.
data: An original dataset of the number of delegates each state sent to each COP, 1995-2014 (COP1 to COP20), collated from the UNFCCC 'lists of participants' (p5 fn5). Regressions use N = 3820 country-year observations (Table 2, p40). Table 1 (p39) gives total, average, median and standard deviation of delegation size per COP. Country covariates (GDP per capita, population, CO2 per capita, democracy, regulatory quality, distance, regions, EU/OPEC/AOSIS membership) come from other sources; GEF data: funds approved per country (N = 2700, Table 5).
method: Counts delegates per Party per COP; the dependent variable is log(delegates+1) by country (p16 fn12). Mixed-effects regression with a random country intercept and fixed year effects (p19). Missing covariates imputed with Amelia II (p20). A second model regresses the log of GEF funds on delegation size lagged 1-3 years (p27, p30-32). The text does not describe how names on the lists were counted or checked: it does not mention badge types, overflow, observer organisations or how organisations were classified.

definitions.definition: Per the UNFCCC Rules of Procedure as cited by the authors: a head of delegation plus other accredited representatives, alternate representatives and advisers as the Party requires.
definitions.quote: Each Party participating in a session shall be represented by a delegation consisting of a head of delegation and such other accredited representatives, alternate representatives and advisers as it may require

definitions.definition: A country that is a member of the UNFCCC; each has one formal vote.
definitions.quote: the UNFCCC formally bestows a single vote on each country (Party)

definitions.definition: The number of delegates each state sent to a COP, taken from the lists of participants.
definitions.quote: an original dataset of the number of delegates each state sent to every COP in 1995-2014

definitions.definition: Countries below a World Bank Gross National per capita Income threshold (as stated in the footnote).
definitions.quote: developing countries are those with a Gross National per capita Income of less than 12,736 USD

proxies.indicator: count of delegates listed under the state in the UNFCCC lists of participants
proxies.quote: State-by-state attendance numbers need to be collated from “lists of participants”

proxies.concept: fossil-fuel interest of a country (country level, not organisation level)
proxies.quote: Since OPEC members have a vested economic interest in continued reliance on fossil fuels
CO2 per capita emissions provide a prominent indicator of mitigation pressures that face a country

findings.claim: OPEC members send larger delegations, controlling for income, population, distance and other factors.
findings.quote: OPEC membership boosts the number of delegates a member sends to the COPs

findings.claim: Countries with higher CO2 emissions per capita send more delegates.
findings.quote: as the country’s average citizen’s contribution to CO2 emissions goes up, so does that country’s presence in COPs

findings.claim: Delegation size varies widely and rose sharply over time; Copenhagen 2009 had the largest total in Table 1.
Larger delegations in the previous year are linked to larger GEF funds.
findings.quote: an increase in one individual in the COP delegation in the year prior to the GEF funds results in an increase of about 2 percent of the GEF fund given to a member state

findings.claim: Per-state attendance numbers are not published by UNFCCC and must be collated from the lists of participants.
findings.quote: UNFCCC releases only aggregate attendance numbers for each COP.

findings.claim: Delegations include non-governmental actors, and earlier work has studied them as a sub-group (civil society, women).
findings.quote: Böhmelt (2013a), which analyzes non-state actors within state delegations

limitations.point: The paper counts total delegation size only. Composition (official versus non-official, including non-governmental actors) is left to future work.
limitations.quote: differentiating the different official, such as ministerial representatives, and non-official

limitations.point: Authors warn that comparing delegation composition across countries is open to misinterpretation.
limitations.quote: cross-country comparison for that kind of an analysis could be prone to pitfalls in interpretation

limitations.point: This is a draft conference paper, marked not to be cited without permission; not peer reviewed as published.
limitations.quote: Draft. Please do not cite without permission.

limitations.point: The paper does not say how people on the lists were counted: whether Party overflow, observers, or business and industry NGOs were included or excluded, how duplicates were handled, or whether the dataset is released. Nothing on business or fossil-fuel organisations is classified.
